newsitem.title: BELGIUM: New supply pact hits EU clearance of Boeing merger.
newsitem.headline: New supply pact hits EU clearance of Boeing merger.

text.p: Continental Airlines Inc.'s decision to buy all its new jets from Boeing Co. will increase the EU's concerns over Boeing's merger with McDonnell Douglas Corp., European Commission sources said Wednesday.
"If this was to materialise ... it simply would add one more element to our worries," one source said, noting that for the moment there was only a "letter of intent" from Continental.

Continental's announcement on Tuesday, which adds to similar contracts signed by American Airlines and Delta Air Lines, will make it even more difficult for Boeing to convince the Commission and rival aircraft manufacturers at a hearing Thursday and Friday that its acquisition of McDonnell Douglas should be allowed.

The Commission said in a recent statement outlining its objections to the merger that it saw the exclusive supply pacts as proof of Boeing's already-strong position in the world's civil aviation market.

European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert also said publicly that the supply contracts, which can last up to 30 years, were unacceptable because they would tie major airlines to a single supplier.

Boeing and McDonnell Douglas will have the opportunity to defend their $14-billion deal before the Commission, competition experts from the EU's 15 states, rival companies and other interested parties on Thursday.
On Friday, it will be the turn of Boeing's only serious rival, European consortium Airbus Industrie, to lay its cards on the table at the hearing.

Its partners, British Aerospace BAe, France's Aerospatiale, Daimler-Benz Aerospace and Construcciones Aeronauticas of Spain, were also expected to submit their views on the impact of the merger on other activities, notably military applications, not handled by Airbus, industry sources said.
Other parties expected to attend include Lockheed Martin Corp. and airline representatives, the sources said.
The hearing will be held behind closed doors and the Commission is not expected to make any statement afterward.
"Don't expect us to say anything. We never do, we're not allowed to," a Commission spokesman said.

The hearing is the last step in the Commission's merger control proceedings before it submits a draft decision to an advisory committee of experts from national competition watchdogs. The committee is expected to meet on the issue on July 4, a Brussels-based industry source said.
The Commission has until July 31 to take a final decision.
